1:
The first word is weighed against the fourth Gospel. Ellicott denies that in the beginning here means from eternity as it does in John, taking it of the beginning of this sidereal system, and holds that since there was never a time when God did not exist, activity being essential to his being, there was probably never a time when worlds did not exist. On the divine name he explains that Elohim is plural in form but joined with a singular verb except of the false gods of the heathen, its root-meaning being strength, and refuses to read it as a plural of majesty, taking it for the effort of early human thought feeling after the Deity and concluding that the Deity is one. Gill reports the dispute over the heaven, some understanding the heaven of heavens, the habitation of God and the angels, made perfect at once and never mentioned again, though he prefers the lower and visible heavens. Wesley and Henry keep to the visible creation, Wesley noting that even in it there are secrets which cannot be fathomed, Henry that the world is a great house of upper and lower stories, every room well furnished, and that the creation of angels is passed over because it is the visible part that is in hand.

Basil the Great sets the tone of his own commentary rather than expounding a clause. It is right, he says, that one beginning to narrate the formation of the world should begin with the good order reigning in visible things, and the creation was not spontaneous, as some have imagined, but drew its origin from God; he asks what ear is worthy to hear such a tale. On the second verse he continues in the same key, that if the fore court of the sanctuary is so grand and the splendour of its portico so dazzles the eyes of the soul, one may hardly dare look into the holy of holies; yet since rewards are reserved for the intention alone of doing good he will not hesitate to continue, hoping with the help of the Spirit not to fall away from the meaning of Holy Scripture.

The formlessness is described by every voice and explained by several. Gill takes it that the earth had a form as all matter must, but not the form it now has, the watery parts unseparated from the earthy, and cites the Targums for a waste and desert. Clarke reports the two Hebrew words as of uncertain etymology but conveying everywhere the idea of confusion and disorder, thinks the Syrians and Egyptians borrowed their gods Theuth and Bau from them and the Greeks their Chaos, and supposes that God first created the elementary principles. Ellicott insists on the conjunction, which defeats the well-meant attempt to harmonise geology and Scripture by treating the first verse as a mere heading, since the two verses form one summary afterwards divided into stages; and he presses the verb, not the copula but the substantive verb existed, expressing duration. Calvin declines to be very solicitous about the two epithets, which the Hebrews use of anything empty and confused or vain, and sets them in opposition to everything that pertains to the form, the ornament and the perfection of the world.

The chaos and the Spirit are treated together. Wesley names the two things the verse gives, the first matter and the first Mover, and observes that the chaos is called the earth though the earth properly taken was not made until the third day, because it most resembled what was afterwards so called, and is called the deep both for its vastness and because the waters afterwards separated were then mixed with it. Keil and Delitzsch note that the writer describes with minuteness only the original condition and progressive formation of the earth, saying no more of the heaven than is necessary.
3:
The form of the divine word is admired before it is expounded. Gill notes that the phrase occurs nine times in the account and that Longinus the heathen admired it in his treatise on the sublime; Clarke gives the Hebrew and says nothing can be conceived more dignified, the words arguing at once uncontrollable authority and omnific power, so that it is scarcely possible to conceive that God should speak more like himself, and he too reports that the Septuagint Greek fell in the way of Longinus. Ellicott makes the phrase metaphorical, there being neither voice nor sound nor any person addressed, and takes it to mean that God enacted a law for the universe; the sublimity lies in this, that God makes no preparation, employs no means and needs no secondary agency. Calvin uses the same clause against a different error: Moses now first introduces God in the act of speaking, as if the mass of heaven and earth had been created without the Word, whereas John testifies that without him nothing was made that was made. Keil and Delitzsch describe the word going forth to the primary material, now filled with creative powers, to call into being out of the germs it contained the creatures which proclaim their Creator's glory.

On light itself Henry and Wesley agree almost word for word: the first of all visible beings created was light, the great beauty and blessing of the universe, which like the first-born most resembles its great parent in purity and power, brightness and beneficence. Henry adds that it was made not that God might see to work, darkness and light being alike to him, but that we might see his works and work our own while it is day; that the works of Satan are works of darkness while he who does truth comes to the light; and that light has great affinity with spirit, so that though we are sure it is, we cannot describe its nature. Wesley notes that it was made by God's word alone.

The approval and the division are read as instruction rather than discovery. Calvin insists that God is introduced surveying his work for our sake, to teach us that he made nothing without reason and design, not that he knew his work good only when it was finished. Keil and Delitzsch defend the wording against the charge of anthropomorphism, man's seeing having its type in God's. Ellicott finds two things indicated, a lapse of time and a verdict of the divine reason, and observes that light was as indispensable for what followed as it was a necessary result of motion in the world-mass. Gill takes the goodness as foreseen rather than experienced, no inhabitants being yet there to profit by it. Clarke denies that the dividing implies two distinct substances, darkness being only the privation of light, and refers the words by anticipation to the rotation of the earth on its axis once in twenty-three hours, fifty-six minutes and four seconds.

The naming and the reckoning of the day close the section. Gill explains the vicissitude by the circling of that body of light, or by the rotation of the chaos on its own axis, giving light and darkness within twenty-four hours. Keil and Delitzsch cite Augustine, that all light is not day nor all darkness night, but light and darkness alternating in a regular order constitute day and night. Ellicott argues that before the distinction was possible there must have been outside the earth, not yet the sun but a bright phosphorescent mass such as now enwraps that luminary, and the earth must have begun to revolve. Calvin says God willed a regular vicissitude of days and nights, withdrawing the light so that night might begin another day, and allows the words a double interpretation, whether the evening and morning belonged to the first day or constituted it.
6:
The second day turns on one disputed word. Clarke holds that the translators, by following the Vulgate rendering of the Septuagint word, have deprived the passage of all sense and meaning: the Hebrew simply signifies an expanse, the space separating the clouds above from the seas below, which we call the atmosphere, though Moses seems to use it more widely, taking in the whole solar system. Calvin likewise knows not why the Greeks chose their word, since the Hebrew comprehends not only the region of the air but whatever is open above us. Keil and Delitzsch derive the noun from a verb meaning to stretch or spread out, and grant that appearance describes it as a carpet spread above the earth, a curtain, a work of sapphire, a molten looking-glass, while denying that anything in these poetical similes warrants the idea of a solid mass such as the Greek poets describe. Ellicott takes the contrary view of the ancient sense: the word undoubtedly means something solid, such being the idea of the Greeks and probably of the Hebrews, appearing in the poetry of Scripture as a vault of molten glass upheld by the mountains as pillars; but here, in sober language rather than vivid metaphor, it means an expanse. Gill agrees: something spread like a curtain, tent or canopy, to which all the passages on the stretching out of the heavens refer.

Henry and Wesley describe the expansion as a sheet spread or curtain drawn out, including all visible above the earth, reaching as high as the place where the stars are fixed and as low as where the birds fly, both of which the chapter calls the firmament of heaven. Henry adds that between heaven and earth there is an inconceivable distance but no impassable gulf as between heaven and hell, so that the firmament is not a wall of partition but a way of intercourse; and that lest it seem God had only commanded the work and another had done it, Moses adds that God made it, for what God requires of us he himself works in us, or it is not done.

The waters above raise the great difficulty, and Calvin meets it directly. Some resort to allegory and philosophize concerning angels, quite beside the purpose; nothing is here treated of but the visible form of the world, and he who would learn astronomy must go elsewhere, since the Spirit would teach all men without exception and the history of the creation is the book of the unlearned. The waters meant are such as the rude and unlearned may perceive: the clouds suspended in the air, which threaten to fall upon our heads and yet leave us space to breathe, restrained by God lest they gush forth with sudden violence and swallow us up. Wesley and Henry alike distinguish the waters wrapped up in the clouds from those that cover the sea, and Ellicott finds this in accordance with science, the atmosphere being the receptacle of the waters evaporated from earth and ocean.

Two commentators notice that this day alone lacks the verdict of approval. Calvin suggests there was no advantage from the work until the waters were gathered into their place on the next day, where the note is twice repeated; Ellicott supposes rather that the second and third days are regarded as one work of separation. On the naming, Gill derives the Hebrew from height, or else from a compound meaning there are waters, while Ellicott observes that our own word is Saxon and means something heaved up. Basil opens his homily on this day by refusing to take from the first the privilege of having been a day apart, not counted in the same order as the others, and praises not the narrator's talent but the grace of Scripture, whose narrative is so naturally told that it delights all the friends of truth.
9:
The gathering of the waters is read both as a wonder and as a mechanism. Calvin calls it an illustrious miracle that the waters by their departure have given a dwelling-place to men, since even philosophers allow that water naturally covered the whole earth; that the seas should be gathered as on heaps and give place for man is seemingly preternatural, and Scripture often extols the goodness of God in it. Gill has the waters, whether on the surface of the earth or in its bowels, flowing as by a straight line to the decreed place broken up for them, and supposes a clap of thunder and perhaps an earthquake which made the cavity of the sea and threw up the hills. Ellicott reads the verb rather of condensation, impossible until the surface had been cooled by radiation; the mass of water now covering two-thirds of the globe had hitherto existed only as vapour, and as the crust stiffened over a molten interior the inner tidal wave ruptured it along lines trending north-east to south-west, whence mountain ranges and deep sea beds.

Henry and Wesley observe that the seas, though many and in distant regions, communicate above ground or under ground and so are one, the common receptacle into which all the rivers run. Henry notes that the earth was in being before but of no use because it was under water, and draws the lesson that many of God's gifts are received in vain because they are buried. Clarke cites Dr Long, who separated the land from the sea on the papers covering a seventeen-inch globe and weighed them, finding nearly three-fourths of the surface water; and he takes the oblate figure of the globe, conjectured by Newton, to bear out the Mosaic account of a mass created fluid.

That herbs and trees came before the sun and moon is the day's chief lesson for two commentators and its difficulty for a third. Calvin says it did not happen fortuitously: God was not ignorant of the law of nature he has since ordained, but did not then use these instruments, that we might learn to refer all things to him. We acknowledge in words that the First Cause is self-sufficient, yet in reality we picture God as poor without second causes; and how few ascend higher than the sun when they treat of the fecundity of the earth. Henry draws the same conclusion, that common providence is a continued creation, and that though God ordinarily makes use of second causes he neither needs them nor is tied to them. Ellicott makes the growth gradual and in three stages: a mere greenness without visible seed or stalk, such as may still be seen on rocks; then the seed-bearing plants, chief among them the cerealia; then the tree with woody stem and its seed in an edible covering. He can scarcely suppose fruit-trees existed before the sun shone upon the earth.

The power of propagation closes the account. Calvin finds the words signifying not only that herbs and trees were then created but that both were endued with the power of propagation, that their species might be perpetuated; Basil hears in the command a natural and permanent law which gave fertility for all ages to come, and traces the stages by which a germ sprouts into grass, receives its articulations, and reaches maturity in the seed; Clarke instances the elm, which produces one thousand five hundred and eighty-four millions of seeds, each with the same power, and asks who can comprehend a single plant. Keil and Delitzsch mark the stage as finished, the earth clothed with vegetation and fitted to be the abode of living beings; Gill ends on the chronologists, who place this day in April or in October as they suppose the world made in spring or in autumn, the Jewish authorities being themselves divided.
14:
The first question of the fourth day is whether the luminaries were then made or only then appeared. Gill reports that some writers, Jewish and Christian, and even modern astronomers, understand the words of their appearance and not their formation; he judges rather that the body of fire and light produced on the first day was now distributed into the several luminous bodies, which are lights produced from that light and instruments of letting it down upon the earth. Calvin agrees that God had before created the light and now institutes a new order in nature, the sun dispensing diurnal light while the moon and stars shine by night: Moses relates nothing else than that God ordained instruments to diffuse the light already made, which was before dispersed and now proceeds from lucid bodies. Ellicott rests the same point on the Hebrew, which distinguishes a light from a light-bearer: there was daylight long before this day, but only now did the sun and moon become fully formed and shine regularly in the bright sky. Wesley calls the earlier light a chaos of light, scattered and confused, now collected and made into luminaries and so rendered both more glorious and more serviceable.

The description of the moon as a great light draws out the strongest statement of method in the chapter. Calvin insists that Moses does not descant as a philosopher on the secrets of nature: he makes two great luminaries where astronomers prove that Saturn, least in appearance because of its distance, is greater than the moon. Moses wrote in a popular style what all persons of common sense can understand, while astronomers investigate whatever the sagacity of the human mind can comprehend; and that study is not to be reprobated. It is not discussed here how great the sun is, but how much light comes to us; to apprehend Moses it is to no purpose to soar above the heavens. Clarke defends the same wording differently, that Moses speaks not of bulk but of the proportion of light shed on the earth, and that those who object that the moon is the smallest body in the system have missed what was said, for it affords more light to the earth than all the planets and stars together. Gill, undeterred, gives the measurements, the sun's diameter reckoned at about eight hundred thousand miles and its bulk at a hundred thousand times the earth, or nine hundred thousand by Newton.

On the stars Ellicott corrects the English: the sense is not that God now created them but that they too were to rule the night, the planets being chiefly meant, so that only on this day was the solar system complete. Clarke explains how lights can divide the night, the sun being monarch of the day and the moon of the night, since rays diffused beyond the earth fall upon the opaque disc of the moon and are reflected back upon the hemisphere opposite the sun. Gill turns the making into a rebuke of idolaters, who worship what God created and set in the heaven to serve purposes beneficial to men.

Henry states the governing principle: these are accounted for not as they are in themselves, to satisfy the curious, but as they stand in relation to this earth, which they serve as lights; though heaven is high it has respect to this earth, and should have respect from it. Wesley lists the uses, the distinction of times and the direction of actions, signs of the weather by which the husbandman may order his affairs with discretion. Basil opens with the circus, where the laws require the spectator to sit bare-headed so that he may be not merely a spectator but in some measure an athlete himself; so in contemplating the show of creation his hearers must bring their own light, and are not so much judges as fellow combatants.
20:
Ellicott sets the fifth day in a pattern: the second triad of days answers to the first, light created on day one and gathered into light-bearers on the fourth, air and water called into being on the second and peopled on the fifth, the dry land appearing on the third and becoming the home of animals and man on the sixth. Basil describes a completed adornment: earth had received hers from her own plants and the heavens the flowers of the stars, the two great luminaries beautifying them like two eyes, and it remained only for the waters to receive theirs; at the command the rivers and lakes became fruitful, the sea travailed, and not even in mud and marshes did the water remain idle. Henry and Wesley note that the work of creation advanced from the less excellent to the more so, teaching us to press towards perfection so that our last works may be our best; fish and fowl were made together and both out of the waters, since the power of the first Cause can produce very different effects from the same second causes.

The verb rendered created raises Calvin's difficulty, since he has argued that the world was made out of nothing while Moses uses the word of things formed from other matter. Those who say the fishes were properly created because the waters could not produce them resort to a subterfuge, the material having existed before; he therefore refers the creation spoken of not to this day's work but to that shapeless mass which was the fountain of the whole world. Ellicott meets the same word from the other side: whales strictly are mammals and belong to the sixth day, but the Hebrew means any long creature, used of serpents, the crocodile and sea monsters generally, so that it marks the great Saurian age. Clarke likewise takes the term as general, comprising whale, porpoise, dolphin, narwal and shark, while Gill collects the ancients on the size of whales, one in the Indian sea five times bigger than the largest elephant, and, on the authority of Juba, some six hundred feet long.

Fecundity carries the rest of the day. Clarke observes that God delights to show himself in the little as in the great, naturalists having found not less than thirty thousand animalcula in a single drop of water, each a perfect animal; and no creatures are so prolific as fishes, a tench laying a thousand eggs and Leeuwenhoek counting more than nine million in a middling cod. Calvin explains the benediction: God does not, after the manner of men, pray that we may be blessed, but by the bare intimation of his purpose effects what men seek by earnest entreaty; and though it seems futile to address fishes, experience teaches that the force of that word has taken root in their nature and constantly bears fruit.

The sixth day opens on the same question in a sharper form. Calvin asks whence a dead element has life, and answers that the miracle is as great as if God had created out of nothing, the material being taken from the earth not because he needed it but that the parts of the world might be the better combined. Henry and Wesley deny that the earth had any prolific virtue or that God resigned his creating power to it. Basil turns the question on the Manichaeans, mad-minded enough to give the earth a soul: at the command it did not produce a germ contained in it, but he who gave the order at the same time gifted it with the power to bring forth. Keil and Delitzsch divide the new creatures into three classes, and Gill notes that the heathen had some traditionary notion of the affair, reported of the Egyptians by Diodorus.
26:
The plural of the divine consultation divides these voices only in tone. Gill rejects three readings in turn: that God addressed the earth, which he calls wretchedly stupid; that he addressed the angels, who are not of his privy council; and that he used the plural after the manner of kings, a way of speaking that did not obtain so early. The words are spoken by the Father to the Son and the Holy Ghost. Calvin says the same more fiercely: the earth, forsooth, was a most excellent adviser, and to ascribe the least portion of a work so exquisite to angels is a sacrilege to be held in abhorrence. God summons no foreign counsellor, and hence we infer that he finds within himself something distinct. Ellicott is more guarded: this is the chapter of mysteries, and in the name Elohim, many powers concentrated in one being, lies the germ of a plurality of persons in the divine Unity, though it is not a formal proof of the Trinity, nor do believers in the inspiration of Scripture so use it.

The deliberation is itself read as a tribute. Calvin observes that hitherto God has been introduced simply as commanding, and now enters into consultation: he might have commanded by his bare word, but chose to honour man so far, not because he paused over a work of difficulty. Man is so exact a specimen of divine wisdom that the ancients deservedly called him a world in miniature. Henry and Wesley take the timing the same way: man was made last so that it might not be suspected he had been a helper in the creation, yet the lateness was both an honour, the method being to advance from the less perfect to the more so, and a favour, since it was not fit he should be lodged in the palace designed for him until it was furnished for his reception. Clarke cites Gregory of Nyssa, that all other creatures are represented as the effect of God's word, but man as the work of God, according to plan and consideration.

On the image the difference is one of location. Clarke argues that God, being infinite, is neither limited by parts nor definable by passions, so that the likeness must be intellectual: God is the fountain whence this spirit issued, and the stream must resemble the spring; the image, as Paul defines it, consisted in righteousness, true holiness and knowledge. Henry makes image and likeness two words for one thing, warning between God and man there is an infinite distance and that man bears the image only as the shadow in the glass or the king's impress upon the coin; it is the soul, in its understanding, will and active power, that is the brightest looking-glass in nature wherein to see God. Ellicott divides the two terms, the image referring to reason and free will and the likeness to man's moral powers and his capacity of attaining unto holiness, both weakened by the fall yet retained in some degree.

Whether dominion belongs to the image is the one open question. Clarke says plainly that it was not, God having created man capable of governing the world and then fixed him in the office; Ellicott allows the body to be after God's image only as the means whereby man attains dominion, erect and endowed with speech that he may give command; Gill counts the dominion part of the resemblance, man being therein God's viceregent. Calvin finds in the making of them male and female a commendation of the conjugal bond, the form of speech implying that the man himself was incomplete, and reads the blessing as the source from which the race has flowed: God could have covered the earth with a multitude of men, but willed that we proceed from one fountain, that our desire of mutual concord might be the greater.
29:
The sixth day ends not in a new creation but in a provision. Henry and Wesley take the herbs and fruits as man's appointed meat, including corn and the products of the earth, flesh not being allowed until after the flood; and add that before the earth was cursed for man's sake its fruits were more pleasing and nourishing than marrow and fatness are now. Ellicott sorts the grant by the classes of plants named earlier: the two more perfect kinds go to man, the birds and beasts receiving every green herb, so that animal life is supplied by the blade and leaf and human life by the perfected seed and ripe fruit. That his food requires cooking, Ellicott adds, has been the basis not only of the refinements of life but of the close union of the family, for what would become of it without the common meal. Gill observes that the words are spoken to Adam and Eve, and that the beasts, wild or tame, are provided for as God's own creatures.

Whether the grant excludes animal death is disputed. Clarke reports Priestley's inference that man was intended to live upon vegetables only, and that, no change having been made in men's bodies after the flood, none is likely in their food; from the same silence it may be inferred that no animal was designed to prey on others, nothing being given to any beast besides green herbs. Clarke adds that before sin entered the world there could be at least no violent deaths, but that by the structure of their teeth God prepared the animals for the aliment they were to subsist on after the Fall. Ellicott agrees that the food originally assigned was vegetable and that express leave to eat flesh came only after the flood, yet holds the dominion already granted had made their use lawful.

The closing review is read as a form of speech, not an inspection. Gill says the survey is attributed to God after the manner of men, as workmen look over their work to see whether anything is amiss, though nothing of the kind can be supposed in the works of God; he notes that Picherellus would limit it to this day's work. Calvin makes the same concession and draws a rule from it, that the Lord designed this judgment as an example, so that none should dare think or speak otherwise of his works, it being unlawful to dispute what God has approved. Henry turns it upon the reader: he who made all sees all, omniscience cannot be separated from omnipotence, and God has set us an example of reviewing our own works at the end of a day, of a week, and of a life.

On the final verdict all converge. Calvin observes that the repetition betrays how wanton is the temerity of man, since once would have sufficed, but God six times inculcates the same thing to restrain our restless audacity as with so many bridles; and now that the workmanship has received its last finishing touch he pronounces it perfectly good, its symmetry admitting a perfection to which nothing can be added. Clarke reads the Hebrew as superlatively or only good, everything formed to the utmost perfection of its kind. Wesley distinguishes the two verdicts, since each day's work but the second was good, while all is now very good because man was made, and because every part being good the whole together is better still. He asks too whether God takes care of oxen, and answers that the young lions and ravens have their meat from him. Ellicott sets this blessing upon the completed work of the Friday beside the last words of Christ, spoken of the second creation on the same day of the week, and holds the verdict to respect man as a species and so not to be annulled by the fall.
